pages.title: adapt: adaptive threshold
pages.short: A separate threshold for every neighbourhood, for uneven illumination.
pages.body:
instead of one threshold for the whole image, each pixel is compared with the intensity of its own neighbourhood, a block of `adapt_block` pixels. this copes with lighting that varies across the image.

it thresholds the **inverted** image, so it keeps features **darker** than their surroundings. (matlab: `adaptthresh` on `imcomplement(img)`.)

`adapt_block` must be odd. larger blocks follow slower variations in background.

pages.title: alpha: significance level
pages.short: The p-value at or below which a test rejects.
pages.body:
a test rejects h0 when p ≤ α. under no real difference, a test rejects falsely with probability about α.

- the dashboard, terminal ui and headless runs default to the value shown below.
- the `evie-mmd-g2image` reference script defaults to 0.01, and prints what it used.

for the gated tree, α is the **total** budget: the gate runs at α and the two marginals at α/2 each. pass the total, not a pre-halved value.

a grid of tests at the same α will show some rejections by chance alone. read the whole [[decision_landscape]], not a lucky cell.

pages.title: Ambiguity
pages.short: How split the decisions are across landmark counts: 0 unanimous, 1 an even split.
pages.body:
for each `r`, the decisions across all landmark counts `n_re` give a rejection rate p(reject) and an acceptance rate p(accept). missing cells, where `r` is too large for that `n_re`, are left out of both. then:

```
ambiguity = 4 · p(accept) · p(reject)
```

- **0**: every landmark count gave the same decision.
- **1**: they split exactly half and half, the least certain the grid can be.

high ambiguity says the conclusion at that `r` depends on how finely the curves were sampled.

pages.title: Kernel bandwidth (sig, median heuristic)
pages.short: The length scale σ of the Gaussian kernel; by default the median pairwise distance.
pages.body:
with `sig = -1` (the default everywhere evie runs a test), σ is chosen by the **median heuristic**:

- the median is taken over the **pooled** sample (both ensembles together), subsampled to 1000 points without replacement if larger.
- σ = the square root of the median **squared** pairwise distance.
- a zero median falls back to σ = 1, with a warning.

any other value of `sig` is used as σ directly.

the bandwidth sets which differences the test can see. much smaller than typical distances, every point looks unlike every other. much larger, every point looks alike. the median sits between the two and is the standard default.

pages.title: Bottleneck distance (diagrams)
pages.short: The worst single move needed to match two persistence diagrams.
pages.body: like the [[wasserstein]] distance, but it takes the largest distance any one point must move instead of the total. it reflects the single most different feature and ignores the rest, so it is stable but coarse.

pages.title: chan_vese: active contour
pages.short: Evolves a curve to split the image into two regions of best-fitting mean intensity.
pages.body:
a region-based active contour. a curve is moved, for up to `cv_iterations` steps, to divide the image into inside and outside regions whose intensities are each as uniform as possible. `cv_mu` penalises boundary length: larger values give smoother, simpler outlines.

it needs no strong edges, so it copes with noisy images where edge methods fail. it is also among the slowest methods.

pages.title: chiral_reference: a reference shape that cannot tie
pages.short: A fixed closed reference with no rotational and no mirror symmetry, for reproducible SST charts.
pages.body:
returns the closed curve `r(t) = 1 + 0.55 cos 2t + 0.30 sin(3t + π/4)`, sampled at [[n_re]] points evenly spaced by arc length, as `n_re + 1` rows whose last row repeats the first. pass it to [[srqd]] as the [[reference_shape]].

a reference fixes every curve's alignment, so its symmetries become everyone's ambiguities:

- **no rotational symmetry**, so a closed curve's starting point is never a tie. a circle, the worst case, leaves every starting point equally good.
- **no mirror symmetry**, so with [[traversal]] `either` the direction each curve is read in is never a tie.

the dashboard and the command-line recipes use it for closed curves, in shape runs and two-sample tests alike. for a grid over several landmark counts, [[shapemmd]] and [[gmmd|shape_gmmd]] take the function itself as `ref_shape`. none of them ever uses a circle.

pages.title: ci_floor: scan-quality cut-off
pages.short: Ignore poorly indexed points; the direction depends on the file format.
pages.body:
scan points of poor indexing quality are excluded before grains are reconstructed. the meaning follows the file format:

- **`.ang`**: the confidence index. high is good, so points **below** the value are dropped.
- **`.ctf`**: the mean angular deviation (mad). low is good, so points **above** the value are dropped.

leave it unset to keep every indexed point.

pages.title: Closed and open curves
pages.short: A curve is closed if it returns to its start; closed and open curves get separate charts.
pages.body:
a boundary traced around an object is **closed**: its last point returns to its first. a path that starts in one place and ends in another is **open**.

a curve is treated as closed in one of two ways:

- **raw**: the input repeats its first point at the end.
- **implied**: you chose the `periodic` spline ([[stype]]). a periodic spline always means a closed curve, so an unclosed polygon is closed automatically. a curve still open after that step is an error.

**closed and open curves are never averaged together.** an intrinsic mean taken across the two is not meaningful, so an ensemble that mixes them is refused rather than quietly averaged.

**don't** expect geometry alone to recognise a polygon that is missing its closing point. it reads as an open curve on both the python and matlab surfaces.

pages.title: cut: remove shapes beyond the convexity radius
pages.short: Drop shapes too far from the mean for manifold statistics to be valid.
pages.body:
with `cut` on, shapes whose full geodesic distance from the grassmannian mean exceeds π/4 are removed. π/4 is the convexity radius, the bound that guarantees a unique mean. the mean is then recomputed, and the check repeats until every remaining shape lies inside it (see [[cut_locus]]).

- it keeps the statistics valid, at the cost of discarding the most extreme shapes. the number removed is itself informative.
- if removal would leave fewer than 3 shapes, the run stops with an error rather than continue.
- in a **two-sample** run, removal applies to the pooled ensembles, so either can lose shapes, and the log says how many from each. it runs separately in each grid column, because each landmark count gives slightly different distances. the per-shape views show the survivors of the last column.
- when shapes are removed, the dashboard can no longer map every shape back to its image outline one for one. shapes and outlines are then shown separately.
- the matlab two-sample scripts do not offer it yet; `g2image.m` does (`cut`).

to see how far out the shapes lie without removing any, leave `cut` off and look at the distances.

pages.title: Cut locus and convexity radius
pages.short: Where geodesics from the mean stop being unique; the π/4 radius keeps statistics safe.
pages.body:
follow geodesics outward from the mean. eventually two different geodesics reach the same point, like meridians meeting at the far pole of a sphere. that set of points is the **cut locus**. beyond it the log map is no longer well defined, so a shape there has no unambiguous tangent coordinates.

on the [[grassmannian]] two radii matter:

- the **injectivity radius** is π/2. the log map is well defined within it.
- the **convexity radius** is π/4, half of that. it is the conservative bound that guarantees the [[intrinsic_mean]] is unique.

with [[cut]] on, shapes farther than π/4 from the mean are removed, the mean is recomputed, and the check repeats until every remaining shape lies within it.

the distance tested is the shape's **full** geodesic distance from the mean, not its distance within the first `r` modes. a validity check that depended on `r` would be circular: removing shapes changes the mean, which changes the modes. so the full-rank distance is the one that says whether the model applies at all.

pages.title: decision_land: rates and ambiguity over the grid
pages.short: Turns a grid of decisions into rejection rates and ambiguity for each r.

pages.title: Decision landscape
pages.short: Every test decision across the (r, n_re) grid, drawn together.
pages.body:
a two-sample comparison runs one test at each point of a grid of [[r]] (modes kept) and [[n_re]] (landmarks). the landscape draws every decision: ○ fail to reject, ✕ reject. it also shows the rejection rate and [[ambiguity]] across landmark counts for each `r`.

it answers a question a single test cannot: **does the conclusion depend on the settings?**

- a landscape that rejects everywhere, or accepts everywhere, is robust.
- one that flips between neighbouring cells shows the outcome hinges on `r` or `n_re`. that is worth saying out loud rather than picking the cell you like.

a known blind spot: at very low `r` the retained modes may miss the difference entirely. accepting at r = 2 and rejecting at r ≥ 4 is a real pattern, not noise.

pages.title: dGr: undulation distance from the mean
pages.short: How far a shape's undulation lies from the mean, within the r modes you kept.
pages.body:
`dgr` is the length of a shape's normal coordinates in the first [[r]] pga modes: ‖t‖. large values mark shapes whose undulation is unusual for the ensemble.

**it is the distance within the model you chose, not in the whole tangent space.** that is by design. choosing `r` is the claim that the first `r` modes carry the structure. a distance that also counted the discarded modes would charge every shape for variation you judged negligible, and it would not change when you changed `r`.

the full distance, over every mode, is used for one purpose only: deciding whether a shape lies inside the region where the model applies at all (see [[cut_locus]]).

- **do** use `dgr` for ranking, clustering and scatter plots: *how far, in the model i chose?*
- **don't** read a small `dgr` at low `r` as proof a shape is near the mean in every respect. raise `r` and look again.

pages.title: dProd: combined distance from the mean
pages.short: Undulation and scaling distances, each normalised, combined into one number.
pages.body:
```
dprod = sqrt( (dgr / max dgr)² + (dspd / max dspd)² )
```

each factor is divided by its largest value in the ensemble before combining, so neither dominates just because its units are bigger. the result ranks shapes from typical (small) to unusual (large) on both factors at once.

because it is normalised **within the ensemble**, `dprod` values from two different runs are not on a common scale.
- **do** compare `dprod` within one run.
- **don't** compare it across runs.

it inherits the rank-`r` meaning of [[dgr]].

for the distance between two curves rather than from the mean, use [[sst_pdist]]. its weights reproduce this normalization.

pages.title: drop_irregular: discard stringy grains
pages.short: Drop grains that are mostly boundary: size below half the perimeter.
pages.body: a grain whose point count is less than half its perimeter is a thin, stringy region, usually an artefact along a boundary rather than a real grain. with this on, such grains are discarded.

pages.title: dSPD: scaling distance from the mean
pages.short: How far a shape's scaling and stretch lie from the mean scaling.
pages.body:
`dspd` is the geodesic distance on the [[spd_manifold|spd manifold]] between a shape's scaling matrix and the mean scaling `p0`. large values mark shapes that are unusually large, small, or elongated for the ensemble, whatever their undulation.

all three spd(2) directions are kept, so unlike [[dgr]] this is the full distance on its factor.

pages.title: edge: Canny edges
pages.short: Boundaries where intensity changes sharply.
pages.body:
the canny detector marks pixels where intensity changes fastest, after smoothing with a gaussian of width `canny_sigma`.

it suits objects with crisp, well-defined edges. larger `canny_sigma` ignores fine texture but can merge nearby edges. gaps in an edge leave a boundary open, and an open fragment is not a closed shape.

pages.title: Scaling eigenvalues
pages.short: The scale of a shape along each of its principal axes.
pages.body:
each shape's scaling matrix `p` has d eigenvalues (two for planar curves). they give the extent of the shape along its principal axes.

their ratio measures **anisotropy**. equal eigenvalues mean the shape is as wide as it is long, like a circle or a square. very unequal eigenvalues mean it is elongated.

they are saved per shape as `evals`.

pages.title: felzenszwalb: graph-based regions
pages.short: Merges neighbouring pixels into regions using a graph of intensity differences.
pages.body: pixels are nodes in a graph whose edges weigh intensity differences. regions are merged while the difference between them is small relative to the variation inside them. `fz_scale` sets the preference: larger values give fewer, larger regions. regions smaller than `fz_min_size` pixels are absorbed into a neighbour.

pages.title: frame_frac_warn: clipped-shape warning
pages.short: Warn when a kept shape has more than this fraction of its outline on the frame.
pages.body: with [[keep_border]] on, a kept shape with more than this fraction of its boundary lying on the image frame triggers a warning. such a shape's outline is largely synthetic. the shape is still kept; the warning is there so you notice.

pages.title: FTE: failed to explain
pages.short: The joint test found a difference that neither part, tested alone, could claim.
pages.body:
in the [[gated_tree]], fte is the leaf where the gate rejected but neither marginal test did.

**it is a disjunction, not a verdict.** either of two things can produce it:

- **pure coupling**: undulation and scaling are related differently in the two ensembles, though each looks the same on its own.
- **a marginal difference too small for the marginal tests to detect**: they run at α/2 on less information than the joint test.

never report fte as "the ensembles differ in coupling" without that caveat.

it is also the leaf most sensitive to chance. under pure coupling both marginal tests face a true null, so a single-seed fte result fails to reproduce roughly 5% of the time. **state the seed** when you report one.

pages.title: Gated decision tree (gMMD)
pages.short: One joint test decides whether there is a difference; only then do the parts say whose it is.
pages.body:
the gated tree explains a difference instead of just detecting one.

- **the gate** is one joint mmd, with a kernel that sees undulation and scaling together (k_f = k_h ∘ k_q, the elementwise product of the two gram matrices). it runs at the full [[alpha]] and asks: is there any difference at all?
- **the marginals** run only if the gate rejects. separate tests on undulation and on scaling, each at α/2, ask which part owns the difference.

the result at each grid point is one of five **attributions**:

| code | leaf | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | no discrepancy | the gate did not reject |
| 1 | explained by undulation | only the grassmannian marginal rejected |
| 2 | explained by scaling | only the spd marginal rejected |
| 3 | explained by both | both marginals rejected |
| 4 | fte | the gate rejected but neither marginal did (see [[fte]]) |

a code of −1 marks a grid point that was never tested.

- **do** pass the total α: the tree splits it itself.
- **don't** halve α yourself, or the marginals run at α/4.

pages.title: Geodesic
pages.short: The shortest path between two points on a curved manifold.
pages.body:
on a curved space, the straight-line path of flat geometry becomes a **geodesic**: the shortest route that stays on the manifold, like a great-circle flight path on a globe.

geodesic distance is the natural way to say how different two shapes are. the distances evie reports ([[dgr]], [[dspd]]) are geodesic distances from the mean, measured through the [[tangent_space]] where the log map makes them exact.

pages.title: gmmd and shape_gmmd: the gated decision tree
pages.short: Detect with one joint test, then attribute the difference to undulation, scaling, or neither.
pages.body:
`gmmd` runs the [[gated_tree]] on one pair of coordinate sets. `shape_gmmd` runs it at every (r, n_re) of a grid, exactly as [[shapemmd]] does for the separate tests (matlab: `shapegmmd`).

all three channels (gate, undulation, scaling) are computed from one pair of gram matrices: the joint kernel is their elementwise product. so the gate costs no extra kernel evaluations.

the results are the aggregate decision, the same binary accept/reject a single test gives, so it feeds the decision landscape unchanged, plus a categorical **attribution** at each cell. an optional audit tests independence within each ensemble.

- pass the **total** [[alpha]].
- report an [[fte]] leaf with its caveat and its seed.

pages.title: Gr_intrinsicmean: the mean undulation
pages.short: Karcher mean of the standardized shapes on the Grassmannian.

pages.title: Gr_PGA: modes of undulation
pages.short: Principal geodesic analysis on the Grassmannian: modes, spectrum and each shape's coordinates.
pages.body:
starting from the mean `x0`, it log-maps every shape into the tangent space and finds the principal directions there. it returns:

| field | what it holds |
|---|---|
| `u_r` | the first [[r]] modes |
| `sigma` | the singular values, the spectrum |
| `t` | each shape's coordinates in those modes |
| `dist` | each shape's full geodesic distance from the mean |

with [[cut]] on, shapes whose full distance exceeds π/4 are removed and the mean and modes recomputed, until none remain beyond it. `kept` then marks which of the original shapes survived.

[[dgr]] is ‖t‖, the distance within the kept modes. `dist` is the full distance, and it is the one the cut uses (see [[cut_locus]]).

pages.title: Grain (EBSD)
pages.short: In an orientation map, one grain becomes one closed curve: a grain is a sample.
pages.body:
an ebsd scan (`.ctf` or `.ang`) records a crystal orientation at each point. neighbouring points belong to the same grain when their misorientation is below [[misorientation_threshold]]. each grain's outline is then traced as one closed curve.

after that, **a grain is simply a sample**. its boundary has the same form as an object boundary from an image, so srqd, pga, mmd, clustering and the dashboard all work on grains unchanged.

- **don't** mix orientation maps and ordinary images in one dataset; it is refused.
- **don't** set grayscale segmentation settings (`seg_type`, `morph_radius`, …) on ebsd input. they are refused with an error rather than silently ignored.

pages.title: grain_boundaries: one closed curve per grain
pages.short: Traces each reconstructed grain's outline as a closed curve.
pages.body:
each grain from [[reconstruct_grains]] is traced as a closed curve, the same way image objects are: smoothed by [[scale]] and filtered by [[min_arc]]. from here on **a grain is a sample** and every later step is unchanged.

fewer curves than grains is normal: grains too small or too irregular to give a usable outline are dropped. curves come back in pixel coordinates. multiply by the scan step to work in physical units.

pages.title: Grassmannian Gr(d, n)
pages.short: The space of d-dimensional subspaces of ℝⁿ; here, the space of shape undulations.
pages.body:
a curve sampled at `n_re` landmarks in d dimensions is an n_re × d matrix. after standardization, the curve is represented by the **column span** of that matrix: a d-dimensional subspace of ℝ^n_re, which is one point on gr(d, n_re).

a subspace does not change when its matrix is multiplied by any invertible d×d matrix. so a point on the grassmannian ignores rotation, reflection, scaling and shear. what remains is the **undulation**: the pattern of bumps and wiggles along the curve. scaling and stretch are kept separately, on the [[spd_manifold|spd manifold]].

for planar curves d = 2; for space curves d = 3.

distances, means and principal directions on the grassmannian are computed with its own geometry (log and exp maps from svds), not by treating the matrices as flat vectors. see [[tangent_space]].

pages.title: grey_seg: one image in, boundaries out
pages.short: Segments one grayscale image and traces its object boundaries.
pages.body:
four steps:

- **crop** to [[sub_reg]], if set.
- **segment** with the chosen [[seg_type]] into a binary mask. objects touching the frame are cleared unless [[keep_border]] is on.
- **trace** each object's outline where the mask, smoothed by [[scale]], crosses one half.
- **filter**: discard outlines shorter than [[min_arc]] or that cross themselves (see [[tol_int]]).

boundaries come back as (x, y) points, in the same column order on both surfaces. the mask is independent of `scale`, which is what lets a scale sweep segment once and re-trace (see [[sweep_ensembles]]).

pages.title: r_vals and nre_vals: the test grid
pages.short: The r and n_re values a two-sample comparison is run over.
pages.body:
a two-sample comparison runs one test for every pair of `r` in `r_vals` and `n_re` in `nre_vals`. each decision rests on modelling choices, so the grid shows whether the conclusion survives changing them (see [[decision_landscape]]).

give either a comma list, `10,50,100`, or a range, `start:step:stop` (`10:20:90` means 10, 30, 50, 70, 90).

cells where `r` exceeds d·(n_re − d) are skipped. every entry must be at least 1. for the landscape's rejection rate and ambiguity to mean anything, give at least two values of each.

pages.title: group_a and group_b: the two ensembles
pages.short: Which two subfolders a two-sample test compares.
pages.body:
each subfolder of the dataset is one ensemble. the two to compare are chosen like this:

- **named explicitly**: those two, in that order. give both or neither.
- **not named, exactly two subfolders**: those two.
- **not named, three or more**: the run stops and asks. taking the first two would silently drop the rest.
- **not named, one subfolder plus loose images**: the run also stops. loose images in the top folder are labelled `root`, and "subfolder versus root" is almost never the comparison intended.

the `evie-mmd-g2image` reference script takes them as `--groups a b`. matlab's `mmdg2image.m` takes them as `groups = {'a','b'}`.

pages.title: Reject H0 / fail to reject H0
pages.short: The outcome of one two-sample test at one grid point.
pages.body:
the null hypothesis h0 is that both ensembles come from the same distribution.

- **reject h0** (p ≤ α): the test found evidence that the ensembles differ. stored as `rslt = 0` and drawn as ✕.
- **fail to reject h0** (p > α): the test did not find evidence of a difference. stored as `rslt = 1` and drawn as ○.

**failing to reject is not evidence of sameness.** it means this test, at this sample size and these settings, could not tell the ensembles apart. a small ensemble, a weak effect, or a poor choice of `r` can all produce it.

decisions are made at every (r, n_re) point of the grid. read them together, in the [[decision_landscape]], rather than trusting any one cell.

pages.title: import_and_segment: a directory in, curves out
pages.short: Reads every image, orientation map or curve file in a directory and returns their boundaries.
pages.body:
the first step of every run. it dispatches on file type:

- **images** (`.tif .png .jpg .bmp`): each is segmented by [[grey_seg]].
- **ebsd orientation maps** (`.ctf .ang`): grains are reconstructed and traced (see [[reconstruct_grains]]).
- **curve files** (`.csv`, packed `.npz`/`.mat`, and with the gis extra `.shp .geojson .gpkg`): the curves are read as given, not computed.

a directory that mixes images and orientation maps is refused.

**subfolder names become ensemble labels.** a directory with subfolders `new/` and `old/` gives two ensembles for a two-sample test. files in the top folder next to subfolders are labelled `root`.

it returns the boundaries, one label per boundary, and per-file information (name, label, how many shapes each file gave, which method was used). files are read in a fixed, sorted order, so runs repeat.

pages.title: Intrinsic (Karcher) mean
pages.short: The average shape, computed on the curved manifold itself.
pages.body:
the intrinsic mean is the point that minimises the sum of squared [[geodesic]] distances to every shape: the centre of the ensemble measured along the manifold, not through the space around it. think of the centroid of cities computed on the globe rather than through the earth.

it is found iteratively. map every shape into the [[tangent_space]] at the current guess, average there, map the average back, and repeat until the update is tiny. the size of each update (‖v‖) is reported every iteration. it should fall towards zero, and a stalled or growing sequence is worth noticing.

the mean is guaranteed to be unique only when the shapes lie within the convexity radius of each other (see [[cut_locus]]).

`x0` is the mean on the grassmannian and `p0` the mean scaling on spd.

pages.title: keep_border: keep shapes cut by the frame
pages.short: Keep objects that touch the image edge, closing them along the frame.
pages.body:
by default, objects touching the image frame are discarded, because part of their outline is missing.

with `keep_border` on, they are kept and closed along the frame edge. each is tagged with how much of its boundary runs along the frame (see [[touches_border]]). the frame-following part is where the image stopped, not the object's true outline.

- **do** turn it on for silhouette datasets. without it, objects that run off the frame vanish, and the ensembles can end up unbalanced by the very shape difference being tested.
- **do** check the tags before trusting a decision.

pages.title: Lipschitz constant (MATLAB only)
pages.short: Worst-case rate of change along a reconstructed curve.
pages.body:
an estimate of the steepest rate of change along a reconstructed curve. high values point to sharp corners or near-discontinuities introduced by reconstructing from few modes.

it is computed only on the matlab surface, and only when chebfun is installed (not under octave). the python surface reports [[rmse]] and has no lipschitz estimate.

pages.title: Mapper
pages.short: A graph summarising a point cloud's shape: loops, branches and flares.
pages.body: choose a one-dimensional filter of the data, cover its range with overlapping intervals, cluster the points falling in each interval, and join clusters that share points. the graph shows loops, branches and flares that ordinary clustering flattens.

pages.title: mask: the image is already a mask
pages.short: For binary images: trace the objects as given, no segmentation.
pages.body:
the image is taken as already segmented: foreground and background, at most two intensity levels. its objects' outlines are traced directly. an image with more than two levels is refused, not thresholded.

this is the right method for silhouette datasets such as mpeg-7 shapes, where every image holds one clean object. silhouettes often touch the image frame, so pair it with [[keep_border]].

pages.title: Merge tree
pages.short: How connected components are born and merge as a threshold sweeps a scalar field.
pages.body: sweep a threshold up through a scalar field. new components appear at local minima (the leaves) and join where two meet (the internal nodes). the tree records the whole history, and its persistence profile is a summary of it.

pages.title: min_arc: shortest boundary kept
pages.short: Boundaries shorter than this, in pixels, are discarded.
pages.body:
every traced boundary shorter than `min_arc` pixels of arc length is dropped before analysis.

the default is small on purpose, so nothing is discarded before you have seen it.
- on large images such as 2048×2048 solar frames, that admits many short contours. raise it (for example to 50, or 200) to compare only the larger structures.
- on small images, a large value can erase the objects themselves.

changing it changes how many shapes each ensemble has. when comparing two ensembles, both use the same value.

pages.title: min_pixels: smallest grain kept
pages.short: Grains with fewer scan points than this are discarded.
pages.body: a grain of only a few points has too little outline to carry a meaningful shape and is often noise. grains smaller than this are dropped before their boundaries are traced.

pages.title: misorientation_threshold: grain-boundary angle
pages.short: Neighbouring points belong to one grain when their misorientation is below this, in degrees.
pages.body:
two neighbouring scan points join the same grain when the angle between their crystal orientations is below this threshold. the angle is **symmetry-reduced**: the smallest rotation relating them once the crystal's symmetry is taken into account.

lower values split the map into more, smaller grains. higher values merge across low-angle boundaries.

pages.title: Maximum mean discrepancy (MMD)
pages.short: A kernel two-sample test: are two ensembles of shapes drawn from the same distribution?
pages.body:
mmd compares two samples by embedding each in a space of functions and measuring the distance between their mean embeddings. if both samples come from one distribution the distance is near zero. it makes no assumption about the distribution's form.

here the samples are shape coordinates: the grassmannian normal coordinates `t` (undulation) and the spd coordinates `s` (scaling) of each ensemble. the [[test]] setting chooses which to compare.

- **kernel**: gaussian, `k(a, b) = exp(−‖a − b‖² / σ²)`. there is no ½ in the exponent. see [[bandwidth]] for σ.
- **statistic**: the biased (v-statistic) squared mmd. under no difference it is small but positive, of order 1/n, not exactly 0. that does not affect validity, because the permutation null uses the same statistic.
- **p-value**: from a permutation test with [[shuff]] shuffles, computed as (1 + #{null ≥ observed}) / (1 + b). it can never be exactly 0.
- **decision**: reject when p ≤ [[alpha]] (see [[hypothesis_decision]]).

pages.title: morph: top-hat segmentation
pages.short: A texture operator: picks out bright structures smaller than a disk. The default method.
pages.body:
a white top-hat with a disk of radius `morph_radius` keeps bright features smaller than the disk and removes the slowly varying background. an erosion of radius `erosion_radius` then separates touching features. otsu's threshold turns the result into a mask. (matlab: `imtophat` then `imerode`.)

**it is a texture operator.** it suits images with structure at many scales, such as solar frames and sem cross-sections.

- **do** use it on textured images.
- **don't** use it on clean two-level silhouettes. with no texture to find, it shatters each object into fragments instead of tracing its outline. use [[mask]] for those.

raise `morph_radius` to keep larger features.

pages.title: multi_otsu: several intensity classes
pages.short: Splits the intensity histogram into several classes and keeps the brightest.
pages.body:
otsu's method picks the thresholds that best separate the intensity histogram into `multi_otsu_classes` groups. it suits images with a few distinct intensity levels, such as phases in a micrograph.

the classes are capped at 5. the search is exhaustive over histogram bins and grows combinatorially: 6 classes can take hours.

pages.title: musketeer: several methods, combined
pages.short: Runs two or more methods and combines their masks by union or majority vote.
pages.body:
each method in `musketeer_methods` (at least two; not `mask` or `musketeer` itself) segments the image, and the masks are combined:

- **union**: a pixel is foreground if any method says so. it keeps everything any method found.
- **vote**: a pixel is foreground if more than half the methods say so. it keeps what the methods agree on.

it is the most robust option and the slowest. each sub-method can take its own settings, overriding the shared ones.

pages.title: n_re: landmarks per curve
pages.short: How many evenly spaced points represent every curve.
pages.body:
every curve, whatever its length, is resampled to `n_re` points evenly spaced by arc length (see [[srqd]]). a shape then becomes an `n_re × d` matrix.

- **more landmarks** follow the curve more faithfully and allow a larger [[r]], at more cost.
- **too few** lose small features.

the arc-length resampling converges at fourth order: doubling `n_re` cuts its error about sixteen-fold. but shape coordinates describe the **sampled** curve, so two different values of `n_re` give genuinely different points on the manifold. that is why comparisons sweep a [[grid]] of `n_re` values and report how stable the decision is ([[ambiguity]]).

pages.title: Persistence diagram
pages.short: Birth and death of topological features as a filtration grows.
pages.body:
as a scale parameter grows, features appear and later disappear: connected components (h₀), loops (h₁), voids (h₂). each feature is a point (birth, death).

points far from the diagonal lived long and are structure. points near it are short-lived noise.

a feature still alive when the computation stops at its largest scale has death = ∞. it is **counted**, because it is a real feature observed alive across the whole range examined. dropping infinite bars undercounts, worst at large scales.

pages.title: Principal geodesic analysis (PGA)
pages.short: PCA on a manifold: the main directions in which shapes vary from the mean.
pages.body:
every shape is mapped into the [[tangent_space]] at the [[intrinsic_mean]], and ordinary principal component analysis is run there. the principal directions, carried back along geodesics, are the **modes** of shape variation: the main ways shapes in the ensemble differ from the mean.

the first mode explains the most variation, the second the most of what remains, and so on. the singular values (`sigma`) say how much each mode carries, and the spectrum plot shows how quickly they fall off.

a shape's coordinates in the first [[r]] modes are its **normal coordinates** `t`. they are what the two-sample tests compare.

choosing `r` is a modelling claim: that the first `r` modes carry the structure and the rest are negligible. see [[dgr]] for what that means for distances.

pages.title: phase: restrict to one phase
pages.short: Analyse only grains of one crystallographic phase.
pages.body: in a multi-phase scan, only points of this phase id are used. ids start at 1; 0 marks non-indexed points. leave it unset to use every phase.

pages.title: pmmd: one MMD test on shape coordinates
pages.short: Permutation MMD tests on Grassmannian and/or SPD coordinates.
pages.body:
given both ensembles' coordinates `t` (undulation) and `s` (scaling), it runs a separate permutation mmd test on each block that [[test]] selects. each test returns its statistic, p-value, decision and witness values.

every test in one call shares the same set of permutations. that keeps the decisions comparable with each other, and makes the answer independent of which code path computed it.

see [[mmd]] for the statistic, kernel and p-value conventions.

pages.title: Product manifold Gr × SPD
pages.short: Undulation and scaling together: the space every shape lives in.
pages.body:
a shape is a pair: a point on the [[grassmannian]] (undulation) and a point on the [[spd_manifold|spd manifold]] (scaling). together they are one point on the product gr(d, n_re) × spd(d).

keeping the two factors separate is what makes results explainable. a two-sample test can say whether ensembles differ in undulation, in scaling, or in both (see [[gated_tree]]). the combined distance [[dprod]] brings the two back together for a single ranking.

pages.title: r: undulation modes kept
pages.short: How many principal modes of undulation represent each shape.
pages.body:
after principal geodesic analysis, each shape's undulation is described by its coordinates in the first `r` modes.

- **larger** `r` keeps finer detail and reconstructs shapes more closely, but costs more, and past some point it fits noise.
- **smaller** `r` keeps only the dominant variation.

**choosing `r` is a modelling claim**: that these modes carry the structure. distances such as [[dgr]] are measured within the modes you keep. so are two-sample tests, which is why a comparison is run over a [[grid]] of `r` values rather than one.

limits:
- `r` can be at most d·(n_re − d) for the landmark count used (d = 2 for planar curves). grid cells beyond that are skipped.
- in a single-ensemble run, an `r` larger than the number of shapes is lowered to 90% of that number, with a warning.

pages.title: reconstruct_grains: an orientation map into grains
pages.short: Groups EBSD scan points into grains by symmetry-reduced misorientation.
pages.body:
neighbouring points of an orientation map (read by `load_ebsd`) join one grain when their symmetry-reduced misorientation is below [[misorientation_threshold]]. the grains are the connected groups. they are then filtered by size ([[min_pixels]]), by frame contact, and by shape ([[drop_irregular]]), optionally in [[two_pass|two passes]].

it is python-only, by design. the matlab route runs through the mtex toolbox, which is proprietary. this gives an independent route to the same grain boundaries, and it becomes the main ebsd route where mtex is unavailable. requires the `[ebsd]` extra.

pages.title: Reference shape
pages.short: The template that fixes every curve's rotation, starting point and direction of traversal.
pages.body:
before shapes can be compared, each curve is rotated (and each closed curve's starting point shifted) to best match one reference curve. with [[traversal]] `either`, the default, the reference also decides which direction each curve is read in. the reference therefore decides the coordinates of the whole ensemble.

**the default is the first curve of the ensemble**, for open curves as well as closed ones. for two-sample tests it is the first curve of the first ensemble. that default is deterministic, but the coordinates then depend on which curve happens to come first. the same two ensembles compared in a different order do not land in the same chart.

- **do** pass a fixed reference when you need charts that can be reproduced across runs. [[chiral_reference]] is one designed for it. the dashboard and the command-line recipes use it for closed curves, in shape runs and two-sample tests alike.
- **never** use a circle.
- **do** make it asymmetric, in two senses:
  - **no rotational symmetry.** a circle, or anything with rotational symmetry, leaves the best alignment undetermined, so the starting point is decided by numerical noise.
  - **no mirror symmetry.** under traversal `either`, a mirror-symmetric reference fits every curve and its mirror image equally well, so numerical noise picks between them. srqd warns when the reference matches its own mirror image. a circle, an ellipse and a straight line all do.

a straight line cannot choose a traversal for open curves: reversed, it is the same line turned half a revolution.

pages.title: Reconstruction error (RMSE)
pages.short: How closely a shape rebuilt from r modes matches the original curve.
pages.body:
each shape is rebuilt from only its first [[r]] undulation coordinates, its scaling and its position (see [[sst_approx]]), and compared with the original landmarks.

the root-mean-square gap is the reconstruction error: small means `r` modes capture that shape well. the error per shape is saved as `err`. the error as a function of how many modes are kept (`err_dim`) shows where adding modes stops helping.

error falls as `r` grows, but a low error is not by itself evidence that the model generalises. beyond some point extra modes fit noise.

pages.title: scale: boundary smoothing
pages.short: How much the segmented mask is smoothed before its outline is traced.
pages.body:
segmentation produces a binary mask. the mask is blurred with a gaussian of width `scale` pixels, and the outline is traced where the blurred mask crosses one half.

it smooths the **mask**, not the image: the segmentation itself does not depend on `scale`.
- **larger** values round off corners, remove small wiggles, and can merge nearby objects.
- **smaller** values follow the pixel outline closely.
- **0** traces the raw pixel boundary with no smoothing.

because only the tracing depends on it, a sweep over several scales ([[scales]]) segments each image **once** and re-traces the saved masks. the results are identical to segmenting again at each scale.

pages.title: scales: smoothing sweep
pages.short: Repeat the whole comparison at several boundary-smoothing scales.
pages.body:
with two or more values, the comparison is repeated at each boundary-smoothing [[scale]], and the decisions are shown side by side. it asks whether the conclusion depends on how smoothly the outlines were traced.

each image is segmented once. only the tracing is repeated at each scale, and the results are identical to segmenting afresh.

give a comma list, `0,1,3,5`, or a range, `0:1:5`. every value must be at least 0. the number of shapes can change with scale, so read the per-scale shape counts alongside the decisions.

pages.title: seed: random seed for a run
pages.short: Seeds NumPy's global random state at the start of a run.
pages.body:
when set, numpy's global random generator is seeded at the start of the run, so any step that draws from it repeats exactly.

the permutation tests do **not** depend on it. they draw from their own generator, seeded to a fixed value, so their p-values repeat from run to run whether or not you set this.

- **do** state the seed whenever you report a result that depends on chance, above all an [[fte]] leaf of the gated tree.

pages.title: Per-subdirectory segmentation
pages.short: Segment each ensemble's subfolder with its own method and settings.
pages.body:
in a two-sample comparison, each subfolder can be segmented with its own method and settings: for example, images from two instruments that need different treatment.

it is available when the dataset has at least two subfolders: the dashboard's per-subdirectory switch, or the terminal ui's "different segmentation per subdirectory?". a headless configuration carries it as `[run.seg_kw_per_label.<folder>]` tables. the matlab scripts do not offer it yet: `mmdg2image.m` segments every subfolder with the same settings.

**different segmentation can itself create a difference between ensembles.** use it when the images genuinely need it, and say so when you report the result.

pages.title: seg_type: segmentation method
pages.short: Which method turns an image into object boundaries.
pages.body:
each method has its own page, with its settings: [[morph]], [[mask]], [[watershed]], [[adapt]], [[edge]], [[chan_vese]], [[felzenszwalb]], [[slic]], [[multi_otsu]], [[musketeer]].

match the method to the image:
- **textured images** (solar frames, sem cross-sections): [[morph]].
- **clean two-level silhouettes**: [[mask]].
- **uneven lighting**: [[adapt]].

if a method fails on some images, those images fall back to another method, and the segmentation summary says which.

it does not apply to ebsd orientation maps; setting it on one is an error (see [[grain]]).

pages.title: shapemmd: the two-sample comparison over a grid
pages.short: Runs MMD tests between two ensembles at every (r, n_re) in the grid.
pages.body:
for each landmark count in [[grid|nre_vals]], it puts both ensembles in one chart ([[sst_tpca]]). then, for each `r` in `r_vals` that the landmark count allows, it runs [[pmmd]] on the first `r` coordinates.

a [[reference_shape]] given as an array fits one landmark count. for a grid over several, pass a function of the landmark count, such as [[chiral_reference]], as `ref_shape`, and each count gets its own reference. the dashboard and the command-line recipe do this for closed curves.

| output | what it holds |
|---|---|
| `mmd` | the statistic at each (r, n_re, test) |
| `rslt` | the decision: 1 fail to reject, 0 reject |
| `tthresh` | the p-values |
| `wit1`, `wit2` | the witness values |
| `sst1`, `sst2` | both ensembles' shape tensors |

cells where `r` exceeds d·(n_re − d) are left empty (nan) rather than tested. the decisions feed [[decision_land]] and the [[decision_landscape]]. the gated alternative is [[gmmd|shape_gmmd]].

pages.title: shuff: permutations
pages.short: How many random relabellings build each test's null distribution.
pages.body:
the null distribution is built by shuffling the ensemble labels `shuff` times and recomputing the statistic. with b shuffles:
- the p-value is (1 + #{null ≥ observed}) / (1 + b), so it cannot be 0.
- its resolution is 1/(b + 1).

more shuffles give finer p-values but take proportionally longer.
- make b large enough that α is well resolved: with α = 0.05, b = 200 resolves steps of about 0.005.
- the `evie-mmd-g2image` reference script defaults to 1000.

pages.title: slic: superpixels, then merged
pages.short: Tiles the image into superpixels, then merges neighbours of similar intensity.
pages.body:
slic first divides the image into about `slic_n_segments` compact superpixels. neighbours whose mean intensities differ by less than `slic_rag_thresh` are then merged through a region adjacency graph, so the final boundaries follow intensity edges rather than the regular tiling.

- **do** keep `slic_compactness` low (around 0.1) on grayscale images. values suited to colour photographs make the superpixels ignore intensity and come out as a near-regular grid.
- raise `slic_rag_thresh` for coarser regions.

pages.title: SPD_intrinsicmean: the mean scaling
pages.short: Karcher mean of the scaling matrices on the SPD manifold.
pages.body: the same iteration as [[gr_intrinsicmean]], using the spd manifold's own log and exp maps (matrix logarithm and exponential). the result `p0` is the ensemble's typical scaling and stretch, the centre [[dspd]] is measured from.

pages.title: SPD manifold SPD(d)
pages.short: Symmetric positive-definite d×d matrices; here, how a shape is scaled and stretched.
pages.body:
each curve's scaling is a d×d symmetric positive-definite matrix `p`. its eigenvectors are the curve's principal axes, and its [[eigenvalues]] are the scale along each. a circle has equal eigenvalues; an elongated shape has unequal ones.

for planar curves spd(2) is three-dimensional (d(d+1)/2 = 3 numbers per curve). principal geodesic analysis there keeps all three directions: a three-dimensional space has no nuisance directions to discard.

like the [[grassmannian]], spd(d) is curved. means and distances use its own geometry (matrix logarithm and exponential), not entrywise averages.

pages.title: SPD_PGA: modes of scaling
pages.short: Principal geodesic analysis on the SPD manifold: each shape's scaling coordinates.
pages.body:
principal geodesic analysis about `p0`. it returns each shape's scaling coordinates `s`, the spd counterpart of `t`.

the coordinates are normal coordinates for the affine-invariant metric. each shape's log map is whitened by the mean (`p0^-½ · p · p0^-½`) and vectorized with the off-diagonal entries weighted by √2. in these coordinates a shape's distance from the origin is its geodesic distance from `p0`.

for planar curves the tangent space is three-dimensional, and all three directions are kept. with no nuisance directions to discard, ‖s‖ is the full spd distance [[dspd]].

pages.title: srqd: curves into separable shape tensors
pages.short: Square-Root Quadrature Decomposition: resample every curve and split it into undulation, scaling and position.
pages.body:
for each curve:

- **resample** to [[n_re]] points evenly spaced by arc length, through a spline of type [[stype]]. closed curves are closed first if needed (see [[closure]]).
- **separate** the resampled curve into a translation `b`, a scaling matrix `p` on the spd manifold, and a standardized shape `xstnd` whose span is its point on the grassmannian.
- **align** each curve to the [[reference_shape]]: its rotation, a closed curve's starting point, and by default the direction it is read in ([[traversal]]).

the results, one entry per shape:

| field | what it holds |
|---|---|
| `xre` | the resampled curve, n_re × d |
| `xstnd` | its standardized shape |
| `p` | its scaling matrix, d × d |
| `b` | its translation |
| `evals` | the scaling eigenvalues |
| `reversed`, `traversal_margin` | under traversal `either`: whether it was read backwards, and by how close a margin |

later steps add `t` and `s` (normal coordinates), `dgr`, `dspd` and `dprod` (distances), and `xapprx` (reconstructions).

a curve that cannot be processed stops the run with an error naming it. it is never silently filled with zeros, which would corrupt the mean of every other shape. an ensemble mixing closed and open curves is refused.

pages.title: Separable shape tensor (SST)
pages.short: A curve split into its undulation, its scaling, and its position.
pages.body:
every curve is reparameterized to `n_re` landmarks and then separated into three parts:

- **undulation**: the wiggles and bumps that remain once scale, stretch and rotation are removed. it is a point on the [[grassmannian]] gr(d, n_re).
- **scaling**: how the curve is stretched along its principal axes. it is a d×d symmetric positive-definite matrix, a point on the [[spd_manifold|spd manifold]].
- **position**: a translation vector.

because the parts live on separate manifolds, each can be averaged, compared and tested on its own. differences in undulation and differences in scaling are then reported separately rather than mixed into one number.

a curve is recovered as `xre ≈ xstnd · p · rᵀ + b`: standardized shape, times scaling, rotated, plus translation.

the fields a run produces (`xre`, `xstnd`, `p`, `b`, `t`, `s`, `dgr`, `dspd`, `dprod`, `evals`) are listed under [[srqd]].

pages.title: sst_approx: rebuild shapes from r modes
pages.short: Reconstructs every shape from its first r coordinates, scaling and position.
pages.body:
each shape is rebuilt in four steps:

- map its first [[r]] grassmannian coordinates back onto the manifold with the exp map.
- align the result to the stored standardized shape (procrustes).
- reapply its spd scaling.
- reapply its translation.

the result, `xapprx`, shows what the model with `r` modes "sees" of each shape. comparing it with the original is how [[rmse]] is measured.

pages.title: sst_pdist: distances between curves
pages.short: Geodesic distances between every pair of curves, with no mean or chart in between.
pages.body:
`sst_pdist` measures how far apart two curves are, directly between their points on the shape manifold. [[dgr]], [[dspd]] and [[dprod]] instead measure each curve's distance from the ensemble mean.

- **dgr**: the principal angles between the spans of the two standardized shapes, which is how differently they undulate ([[grassmannian]]).
- **dspd**: the affine-invariant distance between the two scaling matrices, which is how differently they are sized and stretched ([[spd_manifold]]).
- **dprod**: `sqrt(a·dgr² + b·dspd²)`, with factor weights `(a, b)`, default `(1, 1)`.

no mean, pga basis or truncation rank enters, so a distance does not depend on which other curves were analysed. `dgr` here is the full geodesic distance, not the rank-`r` model radius.

the two factors can have very different scales. the radius form of [[dprod]] balances them by their largest values. that is the weighted product with `a = 1/max(dgr)²` and `b = 1/max(dspd)²`; pass those weights to rank pairs the same way.

- **do** compare curves standardized against the same reference shape ([[srqd]]). both ensembles of one [[sst_tpca]] run qualify.
- **don't** mix closed and open curves; the call is refused.
- **don't** ask for all pairs of a very large ensemble at once: each result is n × n. pass a block of rows at a time.

pages.title: sst_rmse: reconstruction error
pages.short: Per-shape reconstruction error, and error as modes are added.
pages.body: it measures how far each shape's reconstruction ([[sst_approx]]) lies from the original, and how that error changes as more modes are kept. it also picks out the worst-reconstructed shapes for inspection. see [[rmse]] for how to read the numbers.

pages.title: sst_tPCA: both ensembles in one chart
pages.short: Puts two ensembles through SRQD and PGA together, so their coordinates are comparable.

pages.title: Coordinate standardization (stnd)
pages.short: Optionally rescale coordinates by the first ensemble's spread before testing; off by default.
pages.body:
with `stnd` on, each coordinate of both ensembles is divided by the **first** ensemble's standard deviation of that coordinate before the test. the second ensemble is scaled by the first one's spread, so the two stay comparable. coordinates are not centred: shape coordinates are already centred at the mean.

the dashboard and the terminal ui run with `stnd` **off**. the coordinates are already geodesic coordinates in a common tangent space, so their relative sizes carry meaning that standardization would erase.

pages.title: stype: spline type for resampling
pages.short: periodic for closed curves; natural or clamped for open ones.
pages.body:
curves are resampled through a cubic spline, and its type must match the curve:

- **periodic**: for closed curves such as object outlines. it always means closed: an unclosed polygon is closed automatically (see [[closure]]).
- **natural** or **clamped**: for open curves. they differ only in how the spline behaves at the two ends.

space curves (d = 3) must use an open type. closed-curve alignment is intrinsically planar.

pages.title: sub_reg: crop before segmenting
pages.short: Analyse only a rectangle of each image.
pages.body:
each image is cropped to the rectangle before it is segmented, so boundaries are traced only inside it.

**the two surfaces write the rectangle differently.** both describe the same crop:

- **python, the dashboard and `.evierc`**: `((row_start, row_end), (col_start, col_end))`. 0-based, end excluded, exactly like slicing an array: `img[row_start:row_end, col_start:col_end]`. in the dashboard form, type it as `[[row_start, row_end], [col_start, col_end]]`.
- **matlab** (`img_params.sub_reg`): `[x1 y1; x2 y2]`, two corner points. 1-based and inclusive: rows `y1:y2`, columns `x1:x2`.

for example, the crop battery micrographs get automatically (when the directory name contains `battery`) is the same pixels written two ways:
- python: `((150, 850), (0, 1000))`, meaning 0-based rows 150–849 and columns 0–999.
- matlab: `[1 151; 1000 850]`, meaning 1-based columns 1–1000 and rows 151–850.

mind the off-by-one when you carry a crop across.

pages.title: Scale sweep: segment once, re-trace per scale
pages.short: Re-traces cached masks at each smoothing scale instead of segmenting again.
pages.body:
for a sweep over [[scales]], each image is segmented **once**. `build_sweep_cache` keeps the binary masks. then, for each scale, `sweep_ensembles` re-traces the masks with that scale's smoothing and runs the comparison.

only the tracing depends on scale, so the result is bit-identical to segmenting afresh at every scale, and far cheaper. the matlab twin loops `boundaries_from_masks` over scales in the same way.

pages.title: Tangent space, log and exp maps
pages.short: A flat space attached at the mean, where linear statistics are exact.
pages.body:
a curved manifold has, at each point, a flat **tangent space**: a vector space where ordinary linear algebra works.

- the **log map** carries a shape from the manifold into the tangent space at the mean.
- the **exp map** carries a tangent vector back onto the manifold.

the log map is a **radial isometry**: the length of a shape's tangent vector equals its geodesic distance from the mean. distances from the mean measured in the tangent space are therefore exact, not approximations. principal geodesic analysis ([[pga]]) is ordinary pca done in this space.

the honest limit is **scope**, not accuracy. the log map is only well defined out to the [[cut_locus]], so conclusions are local to the mean. that is why shapes beyond the convexity radius can be removed (see [[cut]]).

pages.title: test: which coordinates to compare
pages.short: Test undulation (gr), scaling (spd), or both separately.
pages.body:
- **gr**: compare the ensembles' undulation, their grassmannian coordinates.
- **spd**: compare their scaling, their spd coordinates.
- **both**: run both tests, separately, and report each.

running both says which part of the shape differs. to test both parts jointly, and then attribute any difference, use the gated tree ([[gated_tree]]).

pages.title: tol_int: self-intersection tolerance
pages.short: Numerical tolerance for rejecting boundaries that cross themselves.
pages.body: a boundary that crosses itself is not a simple closed curve, and it is discarded. `tol_int` is the numerical tolerance used when testing segments for intersection. the default is appropriate for pixel-scale curves and rarely needs changing.

pages.title: touches_border and frame_frac
pages.short: Per-shape tags recording whether, and how much, a kept shape runs along the image frame.
pages.body:
with [[keep_border]] on, shapes that touch the image frame are kept and closed along the frame edge. each shape then carries two tags:

- `touches_border`: whether any of its boundary lies on the frame.
- `frame_frac`: the fraction of its boundary length that runs along the frame.

the part of a boundary that follows the frame is **synthetic**. it is where the image stopped, not the object's true outline. the tags are saved with results so you can check before trusting a decision.

**do** check whether clipped shapes are concentrated in one ensemble. if so, part of any difference the test finds may come from the frame rather than the objects.

pages.title: Direction of traversal
pages.short: Whether a curve's coordinates may depend on the direction it was traced in. By default they do not.
pages.body:
a curve can be traced in either direction. segmentation does not always pick the same one: the boundary of a hole is traced the opposite way to an outer boundary.

the alignment in [[srqd]] may shift a closed curve's starting point and rotate or reflect it, but none of these reverses the order of its points. read only in the order given, a curve traced backwards is aligned as its **mirror image** and lands far from the same curve traced forwards.

- **`either`** (the default): each curve is also read backwards, and whichever direction fits the [[reference_shape]] better is kept. a closed curve is tried at every starting point in both directions; an open curve is tried from each end. the coordinates then do not depend on the direction of tracing.
- **`given`**: the points are used in the order supplied. use it to reproduce results from versions without this option.

**under `either` a curve and its mirror image become the same shape.** the alignment includes reflections, so it cannot tell left-handed from right-handed. if handedness matters to your question, trace every curve in one direction (for example counterclockwise) and use `given`.

two outputs record what was chosen: `reversed`, true where a curve was read backwards, and `traversal_margin`, how close the two directions came. a margin near zero means the choice, and so whether the curve or its mirror image represents it, was close.

python `traversal=`, matlab `'traversal'`. under `either`, open curves need quadrature weights and nodes that are the same read backwards; anything else is an error.

pages.title: two_pass: reconstruct again after cleanup
pages.short: Re-run grain reconstruction once after dropping the small grains.
pages.body: after the first reconstruction drops grains that fail the size and shape filters, the reconstruction runs once more on the points that survived. the dropped points are left out rather than reassigned. this mirrors the second pass of the matlab grain workflow, and costs one more reconstruction.

pages.title: Vietoris–Rips complex
pages.short: A shape built from a point cloud by joining points closer than a radius ε.
pages.body: connect every pair of points within distance ε, fill in every triangle whose edges are all present, and so on up in dimension. growing ε gives a nested sequence of complexes, a filtration, whose persistence summarises the shape of the point cloud.

pages.title: Wasserstein distance (diagrams)
pages.short: The cost of moving one persistence diagram onto another.
pages.body: match the points of two persistence diagrams, each allowed to go to the diagonal instead, and add up the distances moved. the smallest total is the wasserstein distance. it is sensitive to every feature, large and small.

pages.title: watershed: basins of intensity
pages.short: Treats intensity as terrain and splits it along the ridges between basins.
pages.body:
the inverted image is treated as a landscape, and regions grow from each local basin until they meet. the meeting lines are the region boundaries. (matlab: `watershed(imcomplement(img))`.)

it separates touching or overlapping objects well. on noisy images it tends to over-split into many small regions; [[min_arc]] and [[scale]] help control that.

pages.title: Witness function
pages.short: Which shapes drive a detected difference, and towards which ensemble.
pages.body:
the witness function is the difference of the two ensembles' kernel mean embeddings, evaluated at each shape.

- **large positive values** mark shapes typical of the first ensemble and unlike the second.
- **large negative values** mark the reverse.
- **values near zero** are shapes both ensembles could have produced.

colouring shapes by their witness value shows *where* in shape space the ensembles differ. that makes it the natural follow-up to a rejection.

witness values are not saved. they are recomputed on load from the saved coordinates and kernel settings.
